opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's changed a lot even in the last few years. When we started having these conversations, there was healthy skepticism. Pharma has seen a lot of waves of computational hype: rational drug design, high-throughput screening, the first generation of AI drug discovery companies. So people had been burned before, and they wanted to see real results, not just benchmark numbers or nice-looking structure predictions.

What's shifted is that the models have started doing things that are genuinely hard to do any other way. When you can show a partner that you designed binders or antibodies against a target their own teams have struggled with, and the wet-lab hit rates are dramatically higher than what they're used to, the conversation changes. It stops being "is this real?" and becomes "how do we integrate this into our pipeline?"

The other thing I've learned is that pharma isn't one monolithic entity. Within any big company you have people who are very forward-leaning, often computational chemists or protein engineers who've been waiting for these tools, and others who are more conservative because their incentives are tied to programs that can't afford risk. Successful adoption usually starts with a champion inside the organization who's willing to put a real program on the line, gets a win, and then that spreads.

So my view now is that the willingness is there, maybe more than people outside the industry assume. But it's earned. Pharma adopts AI when it's demonstrably better on problems they care about, with experimental validation, not when it's a slick demo. That's pushed us to be very rigorous about validating in the lab and focusing on hard, real-world targets rather than toy problems.

r001.rationale: The response says strong experimental results can shift partners toward pipeline integration and that adoption can spread after an internal champion wins. It does not clearly say this triggers rapid scaling of AI adoption.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention time-limited drug exclusivity or pressure from exclusivity to adopt new technologies.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's been really surprising. I came in with a prior that pharma is slow, conservative, hard to move, and in some ways that's true at the institutional level. But the actual scientists and the people running the labs are incredibly eager. These are folks who have spent their careers watching most of their programs fail, and they know the current process isn't working well enough. So when you show them something that might actually change the odds, they lean in. They're not asking "should we do this," they're asking "how fast can we get this into our workflow."

What I've learned is that the resistance isn't really about AI skepticism, it's about trust and validation. They'll adopt anything as long as you can show it holds up in their hands, on their assays, on their targets. And that bar is very high, as it should be, because the downstream cost of being wrong is enormous. So the shape of the partnership matters a lot. The ones that work are the ones where we're actually in the loop with the wet lab, running real experiments together, rather than throwing predictions over a wall.

The other thing that shifted my view is how much domain context they have that we don't. There's a tremendous amount of unwritten knowledge inside these companies about what makes a molecule developable, what the real failure modes are, and that's the stuff that makes the models useful. So it's become much more of a two-way exchange than I expected. They've been more willing partners than their reputation suggests, as long as you respect the rigor they bring.

r001.rationale: The response says pharma partners lean in when a model is shown to hold up on their assays and targets, and ask how fast they can put it into their workflow.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention time-limited drug exclusivity or explain it as pressure to adopt new technologies.

astra-6.text:
Working with pharmaceutical partners has made me more optimistic about their willingness to adopt AI. There’s a real appetite for approaches that can help them discover better medicines. But they’re looking for evidence that it works on problems they care about, not just that it performs well on a benchmark.

So the conversation quickly becomes very practical: Can you design a molecule with the properties we need? Can we test it experimentally? Can you do that consistently? I think what can look like reluctance is often a high bar for validation. If you can meet that bar and fit into how their scientists work, there’s a lot of enthusiasm.

r001.rationale: The response says partners want evidence that AI works on relevant problems and values consistency, but it does not say demonstrated model performance triggers rapid scaling of adoption.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention time-limited drug exclusivity or pressure to adopt new technologies.

sol-6.1.text: Working with pharmaceutical partners has made me appreciate how eager they are to adopt AI when it can solve a concrete problem. The conversation quickly moves from excitement about the technology to practical questions: Can it help us find better molecules? Can we test the predictions experimentally? Can it fit into how our scientists work? There’s a healthy demand for evidence. If you can demonstrate value on a problem they care about, there’s a real willingness to engage.
